title: Programmable passage of macromolecules and gene editors across intact stratum corneum

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reproducible way to move selected large therapeutic molecules across the stratum corneum—the skin’s outer protective layer—and deliver them into a specified living skin compartment without creating a wound. Potential cargos include proteins, RNA and gene-editing systems. “Programmable” means that delivery could be designed and validated for a defined cargo class, target compartment and exposure; it does not imply that every molecule could reach every skin cell.

The intended capability combines passage through initially intact human stratum corneum, delivery to the intended cells, preservation of cargo activity and therapeutically effective exposure. Material deposited on the skin, trapped in its outer layer or transported only through follicles would not establish this complete capability. Existing reports already describe selected forms of intact-skin macromolecule delivery, so the proposed advance is the reliable combination of these properties with human validation and practical treatment coverage.

significance.text: The stratum corneum’s dense, lipid-rich structure strongly limits penetration by large hydrophilic therapeutics. A reliable delivery platform could expand the range of treatments administered locally through the skin surface, including compatible proteins, RNA and gene editors. Within a validated cargo, compartment and treatment area, the direct benefit would be functional exposure of the intended cells without requiring open wounds or physical perforation.

Potential downstream applications include local protein or enzyme replacement, genetic treatment and vaccination. These possibilities remain conditional: crossing the outer barrier does not itself ensure intracellular trafficking, gene expression, editing or clinical benefit. Each cargo would require evidence of activity, appropriate dosing and safety. Delivery alone neither corrects a disease-causing mutation nor eliminates a pathogenic immune-cell population.

The revolutionary significance would lie in making advanced therapeutic modalities usable across clinically meaningful areas of initially intact skin. That impact cannot be inferred from a small-area penetration experiment or a result with one formulation. Transfer to larger areas, deeper compartments, different cargos or repeated treatment would require additional validation. The platform would be an enabling delivery capability, with disease-specific effectiveness established separately.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central target is controlled transport of a defined class of large, often charged molecules through the outer barrier at sufficient exposure to produce a therapeutic effect in a chosen living compartment. The historical 500-dalton rule captures a practical constraint on conventional skin absorption; it is not an absolute physical prohibition on enhanced delivery. Selected successes narrow the challenge, but the supplied evidence does not establish whether the complete proposed capability is available as of November 1, 2026.

The engineering problem extends beyond penetration. A formulation must preserve the cargo’s function, reach the intended compartment, enter the relevant cells and support the intracellular trafficking needed for activity. Gene-editing delivery additionally requires an appropriate functional editing system in those cells. Grada’s broader modality challenge identifies penetration, cellular targeting, intracellular trafficking, expression, therapeutic exposure and safety as connected obstacles.

Route and barrier condition are essential scientific distinctions. Follicles offer a route around much of the stratum corneum, while wounds and physical perforations remove or breach the barrier locally. Microneedles and ablative lasers therefore answer a different delivery question. Electroporation increases permeability through transient pathways and should be evaluated according to the barrier changes it produces. For this concept, initially intact skin and the absence of treatment-created wounds must be demonstrated; temporary permeability changes would need to be characterized rather than assumed harmless.

Proposed engineering requirements include reproducibility across human skin samples and treatment sessions, quantitative dose recovery, practical area coverage and tolerability at the exposure needed for activity. These requirements distinguish a useful platform from an isolated penetration result. Their precise acceptance thresholds remain to be defined for the intended cargo and clinical application.

current_state.text: In June 2000, Bos and Meinardi argued that skin absorption generally requires molecular mass below 500 daltons and described larger molecules as unable to pass the corneal layer. The supplied review verified this historical formulation from the retained abstract. It provides context for the barrier problem, but the abstract does not establish a universal cutoff for enhanced delivery or determine the state of the field in 2026.

Bhat and colleagues’ 2025 review describes chemical penetration enhancers, peptides, nanoparticles and liposomes, alongside iontophoresis, microneedles, lasers and electroporation. It also reports selected macromolecule-delivery successes that the earlier account omitted. In particular, it attributes to Desmet and colleagues targeted RNAi delivery into the epidermis of both damaged and intact human skin using the liposomal carrier DDC642. This is a relevant human-skin precedent, although it is RNAi delivery rather than a demonstration of nucleic-acid editor delivery.

These precedents prevent a categorical claim that macromolecules cannot be delivered into intact human skin. They do not, on the supplied evidence, establish the full combination of therapeutic exposure, a quantified fraction of applied dose, compartment-directed functional delivery, editor activity, reproducibility and practical area coverage without wounds. The review assessment used a truncated retained extraction of the Bhat article; the underlying primary studies and figure images were not inspected. The source index also marks its PDF extraction as truncated. Consequently, the reported successes should be acknowledged without assigning them unverified quantitative performance or broader clinical scope.

Ayman Grada’s article published on January 5, 2026 describes a continuing modality challenge encompassing penetration, targeting, intracellular trafficking, expression, therapeutic concentrations and safety. It supports the importance of measuring delivery and on-target activity in defined cutaneous cells. Its scope is broader than intact-stratum-corneum passage, and it is an account of research needs rather than evidence that this particular platform has been achieved. The supplied review assessed the complete main article; linked supplementary material was not supplied.

The earlier research attributed an approximately 500–600-dalton practical limit and descriptions of wounds, laser microbreaches and follicles to a May 7, 2025 skin-gene-therapy review. It also cited a separate RNA-delivery review. Neither ScienceDirect source has a retained artifact in the supplied evidence, so those source-specific descriptions and the numerical restatement remain unverified here. This access limitation does not establish that the descriptions are false.

The earlier research also presented Vyjuvek as an example of genetic-cargo delivery to wounded skin, but supplied no supporting text for that example. Its specific evidentiary role therefore remains unresolved. More generally, the supplied material establishes substantial barriers and partial delivery precedents, but cannot determine whether the complete proposed capability remains unavailable through November 1, 2026: no bounded current-status search record was supplied.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: begin with initially intact human skin explants and then conduct a clinical study delivering at least one protein above 50 kilodaltons and one nucleic-acid editor into a pre-specified living compartment. The protein threshold, cargo pair and experimental sequence are proposed choices, not established field standards. The study should pre-specify a therapeutically meaningful exposure and measure delivered material as a fraction of the applied dose, cellular uptake, preserved cargo activity and a downstream molecular effect.
completion_criteria.label: Deliver >50-kDa protein and nucleic-acid editor into pre-specified living compartments clinically

completion_criteria.text: Measurements should distinguish material present in a tissue compartment from functional delivery to the intended cell types. For an editor, convincing evidence would include the intended molecular editing effect in those cells; for a protein, an appropriate functional readout would be needed. Local tolerability should be measured alongside activity. These priorities follow the supplied review’s emphasis on defined compartments, on-target effects and therapeutic exposure.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrate functional delivery in intended cells alongside measured local tolerability

completion_criteria.text: Proposed route and safety controls: verify barrier integrity before treatment, document whether treatment creates wounds, distinguish passage through stratum corneum from delivery explained solely by follicles, and assess local and systemic tolerability. Wounded-skin or microneedle results would not meet this concept’s route requirement. A clinically meaningful treatment area should be specified quantitatively for the intended application; the original suggestion of an area larger than a single injection field needs such an operational definition.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrate wound-free stratum-corneum passage not explained solely by follicles

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and breadth criteria: repeat delivery across independent human samples and clinical participants, with independent replication where feasible, and test a second unrelated cargo. Report dose, formulation, tissue compartment, treated area, activity and adverse effects so that the demonstrated boundaries are clear. Success with an additional cargo would support transferability within the tested scope. Finite experiments would establish demonstrated breadth, not universal transport of macromolecules or guaranteed performance in all skin conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Reproduce delivery across human samples and participants with unrelated cargo

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: DER-02, “One-time genomic cure of severe monogenic skin disease through the epidermal stem-cell compartment,” has the closest delivery overlap. DER-04 could contribute a route for a compatible editing system, but a one-time cure would additionally require successful targeting and correction of the relevant stem-cell compartment and durable disease benefit. DER-03, “Antigen-selective erasure of pathogenic cutaneous immune memory,” could likewise benefit from local delivery of an appropriate therapeutic cargo, but selective immune-memory erasure is a separate biological capability. Its title alone does not establish that protein delivery is the required mechanism.

Roster-based synthesis: DER-05, “Epidermal DNA repair sufficient to prevent ultraviolet-driven skin cancer,” and DER-06, “Therapeutic reset of the mutant epidermal field,” could intersect with delivery of repair, editing or other therapeutic systems into epidermal cells. DER-04 concerns access and functional exposure; it does not establish sufficient DNA repair, replacement of a mutant field or cancer prevention.

Roster-based synthesis: DER-07, “A skin-origin intervention that prevents atopic dermatitis and the atopic march,” could overlap through delivery of a locally acting intervention. DER-10, “In situ reversal of established keloids and pathological cutaneous scars,” could overlap through delivery to scar-associated targets, potentially requiring deeper tissue access. Prevention of an allergic disease trajectory and reversal of established scar biology remain distinct outcomes requiring their own evidence.

Roster-based synthesis: DER-01, “Clinical restoration of a complete human skin organ,” and DER-08, “Reconstitution of melanocyte stem cells where the follicular reservoir is gone,” concern restoration of tissue structures or cellular reservoirs. Delivery might support components of those interventions, but passage of a molecular cargo does not itself reconstruct a complete skin organ or regenerate a missing stem-cell population.

Roster-based synthesis: DER-09, “Durable regenerative closure of diabetic foot ulcers after ischemia and pressure are treated,” concerns an existing wound. Delivery into an ulcer could be therapeutically relevant to that concept, but would not demonstrate passage across intact stratum corneum. Conversely, DER-04 would not establish durable ulcer healing or resolve the vascular and mechanical conditions specified by DER-09.

change_log.change: Reframed the innovation as a combined delivery capability while retaining its ID and title.
change_log.reason: The evidence supports substantial barriers and selected successes, but does not establish present-day absence of every form of intact-skin macromolecule delivery.

change_log.change: Qualified the 500-dalton rule as a historical practical constraint and separated it from the unverified 500–600-dalton restatement.
change_log.reason: The retained 2000 abstract supports the historical argument; the relevant ScienceDirect extract was not captured, and enhanced-delivery precedents preclude an absolute exclusion.

change_log.change: Integrated the reported DDC642 RNAi delivery precedent and distinguished RNAi from gene editing.
change_log.reason: The Bhat review contains relevant intact-human-skin delivery evidence omitted from the earlier narrative, without establishing the complete proposed platform.

change_log.change: Separated barrier passage, cellular targeting, intracellular trafficking, cargo activity and therapeutic exposure.
change_log.reason: The review identifies these as distinct requirements; penetration alone does not demonstrate functional treatment.

change_log.change: Clarified differences among follicular transport, wounds, microneedles, ablative lasers and electroporation.
change_log.reason: These routes and permeability changes cannot be treated as equivalent evidence for passage across intact stratum corneum without wounding.

change_log.change: Preserved conditional applications while limiting direct consequences to validated cargos, compartments and treatment areas.
change_log.reason: Delivery can enable treatment development but does not establish disease correction, vaccination efficacy, immune-memory erasure or large-area performance.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to include applied-dose fraction, functional activity, barrier verification, therapeutic exposure, treatment area and local and systemic tolerability.
change_log.reason: These measurements make the intended capability assessable while keeping the numerical thresholds and study design explicitly proposed.

change_log.change: Replaced the claim that a second cargo proves generality with limited transferability and reproducibility criteria.
change_log.reason: Finite demonstrations establish performance within tested boundaries rather than literal universality.

change_log.change: Retained the ScienceDirect and Vyjuvek assertions as evidence limitations rather than established results.
change_log.reason: Missing retained evidence does not prove an assertion false, but prevents using it as a verified premise.

change_log.change: Expanded related-concept discussion using the supplied roster, including qualified links to DER-02 and DER-03.
change_log.reason: The review recommended omitting unverifiable cross-references because those concepts were unavailable to it. Their supplied titles now support explicit title-based synthesis, while detailed mechanisms remain unverified.

unresolved_issues: Whether the complete combined capability was available by November 1, 2026 remains unresolved because no bounded current-status search record was supplied.

The primary studies behind the Bhat review’s intact-skin RNAi and other macromolecule-delivery reports were not inspected. Their quantitative exposure, route, reproducibility, barrier effects and clinical scope remain unestablished here.
The Bhat HTML and PDF extractions are truncated, and figure images were not inspected; additional relevant details may therefore be absent from the reviewed evidence.
Neither ScienceDirect source has a retained artifact. The attributed May 7, 2025 review details, approximately 500–600-dalton restatement and separate RNA-review account remain unverified.
No supplied source text substantiates the specific Vyjuvek example.
Therapeutic exposure thresholds, clinically meaningful treatment area, acceptable transient barrier changes and tolerability limits must be specified for each intended application.
The related-concept connections use roster titles only. They do not establish detailed mechanisms, required cargos or compatibility with a future DER-04 platform.

brief.title: Large medicines delivered through unbroken skin
possible: People could receive selected protein medicines or gene editors—tools that change DNA—through the skin surface without creating a wound. Treatment could reach chosen living skin cells with enough active medicine to work.
why: This could expand local treatment options for people with skin disease. Possible uses include replacing missing proteins or enzymes, treating genetic conditions and vaccination. Reliable delivery across treatment-sized areas would make more kinds of medicine usable through the skin.

sources.showed: Grada describes the connected challenges of getting medicines through skin, into the right cells and working there at a useful dose.
sources.cited_for: Reaching a skin layer is only part of delivering an active treatment to its intended cells.
sources.not_established: This article sets out research needs rather than demonstrating delivery through unbroken skin.

sources.who: J D Bos and M M Meinardi
sources.showed: Their review argued that conventional skin absorption generally requires molecules below 500 daltons, a measure of molecular mass.
sources.quote: the most commonly used pharmacological agents applied in topical dermatotherapy are all under 500 Dalton
sources.cited_for: Molecular size helps explain why the skin blocks many medicines.
sources.not_established: The historical rule does not establish an absolute size limit when delivery methods alter skin permeability.

sources.who: Authors of a skin gene therapy review
sources.showed: This is a review of gene therapy delivery to skin.
sources.cited_for: The review concerns delivery routes for genetic treatments in skin.
sources.not_established: A review of delivery routes does not itself demonstrate reliable, active delivery through unbroken skin.

sources.who: Authors of an RNA delivery review
sources.showed: This is a review of delivery methods for RNA, a form of genetic material.
sources.cited_for: The review concerns delivery of a potential class of treatment molecules.
sources.not_established: RNA delivery alone does not establish gene editing in chosen cells through unbroken skin.

sources.showed: Their review reports earlier work delivering RNA that silences genes into intact human skin using fat-based carriers. It also describes a gel that sustained gene release.
sources.quote:
Additionally, the compos -
ite could sustain gene release over time when combined 
with the PECE hydrogel.
sources.cited_for: Some large treatment molecules have already reached intact human skin.
sources.not_established: These reports do not establish active gene editing, reproducible therapeutic doses or wound-free delivery across practical treatment areas.

shown: Desmet and colleagues, as described in Bhat’s review, delivered RNA that silences genes into the epidermis, the skin’s living outer layer, in intact human skin. This is a precedent for large-molecule delivery, but it does not demonstrate gene editing or the complete treatment capability.
missing: Chosen living skin cells would need to receive a measured, therapeutically useful dose while the medicine retains its activity.
Delivery would need to cross the outer protective layer without wounds and without relying entirely on hair follicles.
The method would need to work repeatedly across people, different treatment molecules and practical treatment areas, with measured safety.

milestones.label: Clinical delivery of a large protein and gene editor
milestones.explanation: Human skin tests, then a clinical study, would need to deliver a protein above 50 kilodaltons, a molecular mass unit, and a gene editor to chosen living layers at measured, active doses. This would establish delivery in people.

milestones.label: Medicines work in intended cells with measured local tolerability
milestones.explanation: The protein would need to function and the editor to make its intended DNA change in the target cells, alongside measured local tolerability. This would distinguish working treatment from material merely present in skin.

milestones.label: Wound-free passage beyond the hair follicle route
milestones.explanation: Tests would need to establish initially intact skin, passage beyond follicles, no treatment-created wounds and local and whole-body tolerability over a defined treatment area. This would establish the required route and scale.

milestones.label: Repeated success across people and unrelated treatment molecules
milestones.explanation: Delivery would need to repeat across human samples and participants with another unrelated treatment molecule, with independent replication where feasible. This would establish reliability and the demonstrated range of use.

uncertain: The dose and treatment area needed for success depend on the medicine and disease.
Acceptable temporary changes in skin permeability and tolerability limits remain to be defined.
Success with selected medicines would not establish that every large molecule can reach every skin cell.
